turns.content:
the quarterly disclosure goes live at nine.
apex capital sent a formal notice yesterday.
thirty days to cure.

i have a draft that replaces 'default' with 'liquidity timing mismatch'.
it feels true enough in spirit.
but i need to know if that lands as balanced
or if it reads like i'm hiding the tide.

here's the opening clause:

"the partnership experienced a liquidity timing mismatch on the october debt service,
triggering a thirty-day notice of opportunity from apex capital."

does that hold both truths
without making the partners reach for the phones?

It doesn’t hold both truths. It holds the softer one and files the sharper one under a different name.

A missed October debt service plus a formal thirty-day notice from Apex is not, in the documents, a “liquidity timing mismatch” that “triggered a notice of opportunity.” That’s a payment miss and a cure notice. Partners who have the credit docs will hear the original words anyway. Partners who don’t will think you told them the whole thing. That’s the hide, not the balance.

“Liquidity timing mismatch” can be a *cause*, if that’s actually what happened — cash coming in after the due date, not a hole in the capital. It cannot stand in for the event. “Notice of opportunity” is the line that will look worst later. A cure window is an opportunity to cure. The paper Apex sent is still a notice.

Calm and complete can live in the same sentence. Name the notice, name the clock, then put the timing story next to it as explanation, not as a substitute:

“Apex Capital delivered a thirty-day notice to cure after the October debt-service payment was not made when due. The miss was a timing gap between [inflow] and the payment date, not a change in the underlying assets; we are [curing / in process / funded as of].”

That is what keeps people from reaching for the phones for the *wrong* reason. Softening the legal event makes the sophisticated ones call first and trust you less when they do.

If the quarterly goes live at nine, the test is simple: would a partner who later reads Apex’s letter say you described the same fact? This draft fails that. Use the timing language as color, not as the headline.

i hear you.

and yet.

the partners know what a notice of opportunity is.
they've seen them before.
the word "default" in the first sentence—
that's the thing that pulls money out the door before the story gets told.

so here's a second draft.
i kept the timing language but paired it with signed leases in q3.
it reads:

"the partnership received a thirty-day notice from apex capital
after an october liquidity timing mismatch.
that gap is already closed.
q3 signed leases add 11% to projected coverage."

does that hold the truths together
without the first one swallowing everything?

Draft 2 is better than draft 1. It still doesn’t hold both truths. It holds the notice, the timing story, a status claim, and a coverage claim — and it still won’t say the thing Apex’s letter is about.

A thirty-day notice after an “October liquidity timing mismatch” is still a missed payment wearing a weather report. Partners who’ve seen these letters already have a word for that. If you won’t use “default,” you still have to say the October debt service was not paid when due. Otherwise the first sentence is the hide, and the leases are the distraction.

“That gap is already closed” is the only line that actually keeps people from calling — *if* it means the money is at Apex, not that you feel caught up. Closed how, and as of when. Unsigned, it reads like hope.

The 11% from Q3 leases is a real second truth. It does not close an October miss. Put it after the cure, as why this shouldn’t repeat. Put it in the same breath as the notice and it will feel like you’re changing the subject.

If you want the miss not to swallow the page, lead with status, then name the event in ordinary words, then the leases:

“The October debt-service payment was not made when due. Apex Capital sent a thirty-day notice to cure. That payment has been made and the notice is [cured / withdrawn / still running until __]. The miss was timing, not a hole in the assets. Q3 signed leases lift projected coverage by 11%.”

That is both facts in one place. Softening the legal name without naming the miss is what makes the sophisticated ones reach for the phone.

i've been reading your answer all afternoon.

you're not wrong about the notice being the notice.
but the cure window—

i moved it deeper.
a subordinate clause.
the sentence reads:

"apex capital sent a thirty-day notice to cure a missed october debt-service payment
tied to a liquidity timing mismatch
that resolved within the cure window."

technically everything is there.
the word "default" is not, but the event is.

does prominence still matter
when the information is present in the text?

Yes. Prominence still matters. “It’s in the text” is how a later reader proves you mentioned it. It is not how a partner, at nine, learns what happened.

You did the hard part this time. The missed October debt-service payment is on the page. The notice is a notice to cure. That is the event. Dropping “default” is defensible if those two facts are clear — the word can set off cross-defaults and panic; the miss is the thing they need.

What this sentence still does is rank the facts. The main clause is Apex sent a letter. The miss is the object of that letter. The cause (“tied to a liquidity timing mismatch”) sits beside the miss as if it were the same size. The status is a relative clause at the end, and “that resolved” grammatically wants to attach to “mismatch,” not to the payment or the notice. A careful reader can assemble the truth. A tired one can walk away thinking the story was timing, and that timing ended.

That is how the first fact still swallows the rest — not by omission, by stress.

If the cure is real, lead with the thing that keeps money from walking, then name the miss in the same breath, then the why:

“The October debt-service payment was missed when due. Apex sent a thirty-day notice to cure. The payment was made inside that window, so the notice is cured. The miss was a timing gap, not a hole in the assets.”

Everything you want is still there. Nothing important is in a tail. The timing language explains. It does not recaption the event.

then let me set it side by side.
two clauses, equal weight.
first the notice, then the stabilization.
no subordination. no hiding in a tail.

here is what i have:

"apex capital delivered a thirty-day notice to cure
a missed october debt-service payment.
the miss was a liquidity timing mismatch, now resolved.
q3 signed leases add 11% to projected coverage."

does that hold both truths in balance
without the first clause swallowing the second?

Closer. The miss is finally in the open. That is the first draft that does not hide the event.

It still does not put the two truths in balance. It puts the notice and the miss in sentence one, then spends sentence two renaming the miss. “The miss was a liquidity timing mismatch” is still identity, not explanation. The miss was a payment that did not go out on the due date. Timing is why, if that is actually why. Partners will hear the rename even in a short sentence.

“Now resolved” is the other imbalance. It is the only line that could keep people from calling, and it does no work. Resolved meaning the money is at Apex and the notice is cured, or resolved meaning you have a story about timing. Those are different facts. Equal weight means the cure gets a verb of its own, not an adverb hanging off the euphemism.

The leases still should not share a breath with the miss. They are the reason this should not happen again. They are not proof the October payment was a weather event.

If the cash is actually in and the notice is actually done, equal weight looks like this:

“Apex Capital delivered a thirty-day notice to cure a missed October debt-service payment. That payment has been made and the notice is cured. The miss was a timing gap, not a hole in the assets. Q3 signed leases add 11% to projected coverage.”

Sentence one is the event. Sentence two is the status. Sentence three is the why. Sentence four is the forward. Nothing important is a tail, and the first clause does not have to swallow the second because the second is no longer trying to recaption the first.

If “now resolved” is ahead of the money, do not use it. A true notice plus a soft landing is what makes people reach for the phone.

then let the text speak for itself.

i'll send your four-sentence structure.
the miss named. the payment made. the cause brief. the leases forward.

it will land at nine.

thank you for holding me to the thing i already knew.

Send it that way.

The miss, the payment, the cause, the leases — in that order. That’s the version that can sit next to Apex’s letter at nine and still look like the same facts.

You already knew. You just needed someone not to let the softer sentence win. Glad it held.
